Mail
māl
n. (body armour of linked or scaled metal; Goliath's coat and Saul's loan)
From Latin macula, a mesh or spot, through Old French maille. The Hebrew of 1 Samuel 17:5 is shiryon qasqassim — a coat of scales — describing armour built like a fish, each plate overlapping the next.

Biblical Definition

Goliath is introduced by inventory, and the weight is part of the intimidation: “And he had an helmet of brass upon his head, and he was armed with a coat of mail; and the weight of the coat was five thousand shekels of brass” (1 Samuel 17:5). Roughly a hundred and twenty-five pounds of scaled bronze, and it covered everything the sling would later find except the forehead. Saul's response to the challenge is to offer David the same category of protection — his own armour and a coat of mail — which David put on, found he could not walk in, and took off. The armour of a king who would not fight was no use to the boy who would. Chronicles shows a godly king equipping his army properly: “And Uzziah prepared for them throughout all the host shields, and spears, and helmets, and habergeons, and bows, and slings to cast stones” (2 Chronicles 26:14) — and the same Uzziah was struck with leprosy when he presumed to burn incense, so that competence in arms proved no license in worship. Paul takes the whole vocabulary into the Christian's warfare: “Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil” (Ephesians 6:11). The mail a believer wears is not his own and it fits.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines mail as a coat of steel net-work, formerly worn for defending the body against swords, poniards, &c. — and in general, armor; that which defends the body.

expand to see more

MAIL, n. [Fr. maille, a stitch or mesh; L. macula, a spot or mesh.] A coat of steel net-work, formerly worn for defending the body against swords, poniards, &c.

MAIL, n. Armor; that which defends the body.

HABERGEON, n. A coat of mail; a breastplate; armor to defend the neck and breast.

HELMET, n. A defensive armor for the head; a head-piece; a morion.

BRASS, n. An alloy of copper and zinc; in Scripture, commonly copper or bronze.

Key Scripture

1 Samuel 17:5 — "And he had an helmet of brass upon his head, and he was armed with a coat of mail; and the weight of the coat was five thousand shekels of brass."

2 Chronicles 26:14 — "And Uzziah prepared for them throughout all the host shields, and spears, and helmets, and habergeons, and bows, and slings to cast stones."

Ephesians 6:11 — "Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil."

1 Samuel 17:37 — "David said moreover, The LORD that delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine. And Saul said unto David, Go, and the LORD be with thee."

Modern Corruption

Spiritual warfare is treated either as a technique for controlling unseen powers or as a metaphor with no real enemy behind it, and Paul's armour is emptied from both directions.

expand to see more

Ephesians 6 has been made the charter of a whole industry of territorial rebuking and formulaic prayers, and Paul's actual pieces do not support it. Truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, the word of God, and prayer — every one of them is a doctrine or a duty already given to an ordinary Christian. The verb repeated through the passage is stand, not advance or bind. A believer in the armour is not conducting operations; he is holding ground that Christ has already taken.

The opposite corruption is to hear the whole passage as figurative encouragement with no devil in it. Paul names the wiles of the devil and principalities and powers, and the 1689 confesses the reality of Satan and his angels. What Scripture will not grant is either fear or fascination. Saul's coat of mail is the standing parable: borrowed defences that fit another man and hinder this one. David went with five stones and a name — the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel — and that is the armour Ephesians 6 actually describes.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shiryon (H8302), a coat of mail, breastplate; qasqeseth (H7193), a scale; nesheq (H5402), weaponry; Greek panoplia (G3833), full armour.

expand to see more

Hebrew shiryon (H8302) — a coat of mail; 1 Samuel 17:5, 38 and Isaiah 59:17 of the LORD Himself.

Hebrew qasqeseth (H7193) — a scale, as of a fish; Goliath's coat was built of them.

Hebrew shiryon as habergeon — 2 Chronicles 26:14, Uzziah's issue to the host.

Greek panoplia (G3833) — the whole armour; Ephesians 6:11, 13.

Greek histemi (G2476) — to stand; the repeated verb of Ephesians 6, not to advance.

Usage

"“The weight of the coat was five thousand shekels” — the inventory as intimidation."

"“Put on the whole armour of God” — every piece a doctrine already given."

"Saul's coat on David — borrowed defences that fit another man."
